title: Chapter 5 Mastery Quiz: Sensory & Motor Systems
description: Test your mastery of sensory transduction, retinal pathways, dual visual streams, audition, somatosensory homunculus, gate control theory, and motor tracts.

questions.question: What is the biological definition of 'sensory transduction'?

options.text: The transformation of physical environmental energy into electrical receptor potentials
The conscious emotional appraisal of a sensory memory
The voluntary motor command sent to a contracting muscle
The transport of cerebrospinal fluid through the central canal

questions.explanation: Transduction converts physical stimuli (light, pressure, chemicals) into neuronal graded potentials.

questions.question: Which photoreceptors are concentrated in the central fovea and are responsible for high-acuity color vision in daylight?

options.text: Cones
Rods
Pacinian corpuscles
Horizontal cells

questions.explanation: Cones mediate photopic (daylight) high-acuity color vision and are packed densely in the fovea centralis.

questions.question: Rods differ fundamentally from cones in that rods:

options.text: Possess extreme light sensitivity, operate in dim light, and exhibit high neural convergence
Contain three distinct photopigments for red, green, and blue
Are found exclusively inside the fovea centralis
Synapse directly onto corticospinal motor neurons

questions.explanation: Rods operate in scotopic (dim) lighting, lack color discrimination, and exhibit high convergence onto ganglion cells.

questions.question: What causes the physiological 'blind spot' in each human eye?

options.text: The optic disc where ganglion cell axons bundle to exit the eye as the optic nerve, devoid of photoreceptors
A natural tear in the corneal epithelium
Excessive density of rods blocking incoming photons
The shadow cast by the iris under bright light

questions.explanation: The optic disc contains no rods or cones because it is the exit point for the optic nerve bundle.

questions.question: At the Optic Chiasm, what happens to axons originating from the nasal hemiretinas?

options.text: They cross the midline to the contralateral optic tract
They continue straight without crossing on the ipsilateral side
They terminate in the olfactory bulb
They synapse directly onto the primary motor cortex

questions.explanation: Nasal hemiretina axons decussate at the chiasm, while temporal hemiretina axons stay uncrossed.

questions.question: What Nobel Prize-winning feature did David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel discover about Primary Visual Cortex (V1) neurons?

options.text: They respond selectively to bars and edges of specific orientations
They respond exclusively to pure diffuse circular light flashes
They fire only when the subject is completely asleep
They can directly synthesize glucose from sunlight

questions.explanation: Hubel & Wiesel demonstrated that V1 simple and complex cortical neurons act as feature detectors tuned to oriented bars and edges.

questions.question: The Dorsal Visual Stream projects from V1 toward which cortical destination?

options.text: Posterior parietal cortex ('Where / How' pathway)
Inferior temporal cortex ('What' pathway)
Broca's area exclusively
Primary somatosensory postcentral gyrus

questions.explanation: The dorsal stream terminates in the posterior parietal cortex, governing spatial awareness and visually guided action.

questions.question: Akinetopsia (the selective inability to perceive fluid visual motion) is caused by damage to which cortical visual area?

options.text: Area MT / V5
Area V4
Fusiform Face Area
Primary auditory cortex

questions.explanation: Cortical area MT/V5 in the dorsal stream is specialized for motion processing; bilateral lesions produce motion blindness (akinetopsia).

questions.question: Visual Object Agnosia (inability to recognize objects visually despite intact visual acuity) results from damage to:

options.text: The ventral visual stream in the inferior temporal cortex
The dorsal visual stream in the parietal lobe
The optic chiasm exclusively
The semicircular canals of the inner ear

questions.explanation: Damage to the ventral 'what' pathway in the inferior temporal cortex produces apperceptive or associative visual agnosia.

questions.question: The three auditory ossicles that amplify sound pressure in the middle ear are the:

options.text: Malleus (hammer), Incus (anvil), and Stapes (stirrup)
Cochlea, Vestibule, and Semicircular canal
Tympanum, Pinna, and Lobule
Dura, Arachnoid, and Pia

questions.explanation: The malleus, incus, and stapes form an impedance-matching mechanical lever system amplifying airborne vibrations onto the oval window.

questions.question: What mechanically gated ion influx directly depolarizes inner hair cells in the cochlea when stereocilia deflect?

options.text: Potassium (K+) influx from the high-potassium endolymph
Chloride (Cl-) influx
Hydrogen ion influx
Magnesium ion efflux

questions.explanation: Endolymph surrounding stereocilia has an unusually high K+ concentration (~150 mM); opening tip link channels drives K+ into hair cells, causing depolarization.

questions.question: Tonotopic organization of the basilar membrane dictates that low-frequency sounds (e.g., 50 Hz) maximally displace:

options.text: The wide, flexible apex of the cochlea near the helicotrema
The narrow, stiff base near the oval window
The ossicles in the middle ear only
The auditory nerve sheath

questions.explanation: Low frequencies travel to the wide, floppy cochlear apex before causing peak basilar membrane displacement.

questions.question: In Wilder Penfield's Sensory Homunculus, why do the human hands and lips occupy vastly more cortical area than the back or legs?

options.text: They possess an exceptionally high density of sensory receptors with small receptive fields (cortical magnification)
They contain more bone mass than the trunk
They receive direct blood flow from the carotid artery without capillaries
Their sensory neurons have no myelin sheaths

questions.explanation: Cortical magnification reflects the disproportionate number of sensory afferents and fine discrimination capacity of hands and lips.

questions.question: Which cutaneous mechanoreceptor adapts rapidly and is exquisitely sensitive to high-frequency vibrations (e.g., 250 Hz)?

options.text: Pacinian corpuscle
Merkel disc
Ruffini ending
Free nerve ending

questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles have concentric lamellar onion-like capsules that filter static pressure, responding maximally to rapid vibrations.

questions.question: Fast, sharp, localized 'first pain' is conducted to the central nervous system via which fibers?

options.text: A-delta (Aδ) fibers
Unmyelinated C fibers
A-alpha fibers
Postganglionic sympathetic fibers

questions.explanation: Lightly myelinated A-delta fibers conduct initial sharp pain rapidly, whereas unmyelinated C fibers conduct slow, dull, burning secondary pain.

questions.question: According to the Gate Control Theory of pain, descending analgesic signals from the brainstem periaqueductal gray (PAG) suppress pain by:

options.text: Releasing endogenous endorphins and activating inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord dorsal horn
Severing the peripheral motor nerves
Shutting down all brain oxygen consumption
Paralyzing the vocal cords so the person cannot complain

questions.explanation: PAG activation drives descending serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways that stimulate enkephalinergic spinal interneurons to close the pain gate.

questions.question: What type of neurons in the premotor cortex fire both when executing an action and when observing another individual perform that same action?

options.text: Mirror neurons
Purkinje cells
Betz cells
Granule cells

questions.explanation: Mirror neurons, discovered by Rizzolatti et al., provide a potential neural substrate for action understanding, imitation, and empathy.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of fibers in the human corticospinal tract cross the midline at the medullary pyramidal decussation?

options.text: Approximately 85% to 90%
Exactly 100%
Only 10%
Fibers never cross the midline

questions.explanation: About 90% of corticospinal axons cross in the medullary pyramids to form the lateral corticospinal tract.

questions.question: A patient with an Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) lesion (e.g., following a cortical stroke) typically exhibits:

options.text: Spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a positive Babinski sign
Flaccid paralysis, absent reflexes, and severe rapid muscle fasciculations
Total loss of pain sensation with completely normal motor tone
Intention tremor only without any weakness

questions.explanation: UMN damage removes descending cortical inhibition, resulting in spastic hypertonia, hyperactive deep tendon reflexes, and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response.

questions.question: A Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) lesion affecting the ventral horn motor cells produces:

options.text: Flaccid paralysis, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and hyporeflexia
Clasp-knife spastic rigidity and hyperreflexia
Resting pill-rolling tremor and chorea
Loss of short-term declarative memory

questions.explanation: LMN lesions disconnect muscles from nervous input entirely, causing flaccid paralysis, loss of reflexes, fasciculations, and severe denervation atrophy.

questions.question: What is Weber's Law in sensory psychophysics?

options.text: The Just Noticeable Difference (JND) is a constant proportion of the initial stimulus intensity (ΔI / I = k)
Sensory perception increases as an exponential square of action potential velocity
All sensory modalities travel along the exact same speed in unmyelinated axons
Pain thresholds are identical in all human beings regardless of age

questions.explanation: Weber's Law states that the ratio of the increment threshold to the background intensity is a constant fraction across sensory dimensions.

questions.question: Prosopagnosia is a selective neurovisual deficit characterized by the inability to:

options.text: Recognize familiar human faces, despite preserved ability to recognize other common objects
Perceive visual objects moving across the visual field
Distinguish between red and green colors
Guide the hand to reach out and grasp an object in space

questions.explanation: Prosopagnosia ('face blindness') results from lesions to the fusiform face area (FFA) in the ventral temporal cortex.
